meta.title: Who really said "It is double pleasure to deceive the deceiver"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Machiavelli. It closes La Fontaine's fable "Le Coq et le Renard" (Fables, Book II.15, 1668): "Car c'est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is double pleasure to deceive the deceiver'?
meta.ogDescription: Machiavelli never wrote it. The line is La Fontaine's — the closing moral of "The Cock and the Fox," Fables, Book II, fable 15, 1668.

answer.label: Not Machiavelli — actually Jean de La Fontaine
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is the closing moral of La Fontaine’s fable “Le Coq et le Renard” (The Cock and the Fox), Fables, Book II, fable 15, first published in 1668: “Car c’est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur.” Wikiquote files the English version under Machiavelli’s misattributed quotes ↗ and finds no origin for it in his texts.

source.heading: The fable it actually ends

docMeta.dd: Fables, Book II, fable 15 — “Le Coq et le Renard”
1668 (Books I–VI); the digitised Thierry & Barbin printing linked here is 1678
Car c’est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur.
The English wording that circulates online carries no translator credit. Elizur Wright’s 19th-century verse translation renders the close as “’Tis doubly sweet deceiver to deceive.”

source.excerpt:
… Mal content de son stratagème.
Et notre vieux coq en soi-même
Se mit à rire de sa peur ;
Car c’est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur.
trail: Wikiquote’s Machiavelli page ↗ lists “It is double pleasure to deceive the deceiver” under Misattributed, noting that it does not originate from his texts, has been popularised by internet sources, and is more than likely a variant of a line from La Fontaine’s Fables.
Wikiquote’s La Fontaine page ↗ sources the French original, “C’est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur,” to Book II (1668), fable 15, “The Cock and the Fox.”

The line is there in the printed text: the 1874 Bernardin-Béchet edition on Wikisource ↗ prints fable XV of Book II ending on exactly that verse, and the 1678 Thierry & Barbin printing ↗ carries it at pp. 122–124.

Nineteenth-century English readers met it differently: Elizur Wright’s verse translation ↗ ends “The cock laugh’d sweetly in his sleeve;— ’Tis doubly sweet deceiver to deceive.” The tidier modern sentence has no translator attached to it.
source.excerptNote: In the fable, a fox tries to coax an old cock down from his branch with news that universal peace has been declared. The cock says he is delighted — and adds that two greyhounds are running towards them, no doubt carrying the same happy news. The fox bolts. The English sentence people quote under Machiavelli’s name is a flat literal rendering of that last line; Wikiquote gives it as “It is a double pleasure to deceive the deceiver” ↗.

author.name: Jean de La Fontaine
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Jean de La Fontaine
author.bio: La Fontaine spent three decades turning Aesop, Indian folklore and Renaissance emblem books into supple French verse, publishing his Fables in instalments from 1668 onward. His animals are courtiers in feathers: the fox flatters, the cock calculates, and the moral lands in a single closing line built to be memorised. That habit of ending on an epigram is exactly why so many of his last lines now float free of the fables they belong to.

cite.sourceCitation: Jean de La Fontaine, “Le Coq & le Renard,” in Fables choisies, mises en vers, Book II, fable 15 (Paris: Denys Thierry et Claude Barbin, 1678), tome premier, pp. 122–124; the fable first appeared in the 1668 collection of Books I–VI. English verse translation: Fables of La Fontaine, trans. Elizur Wright, new edition with notes by J. W. M. Gibbs (translation first published Boston, 1841; preface to this edition dated London, 1881), “The Cock and the Fox.”

copyAttribution: "It is double pleasure to deceive the deceiver" is not Machiavelli. The line is Jean de La Fontaine's — "Car c'est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur" — the closing moral of "Le Coq et le Renard," Fables, Book II, fable 15, first published 1668. Wikiquote lists the English version under Machiavelli's misattributed quotes. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: How Machiavelli got the credit
misattribution.intro: The thought is cynical, compact and about outfoxing a manipulator, which is more or less the job description the internet has assigned to Machiavelli. So the sentence gets dressed in his name — on quote aggregators, on posters, and even in the title of a peer-reviewed psychology paper.

items.why: Wikiquote places it in the Misattributed section ↗ of his page, stating that it does not originate from his texts and is more than likely a variant of a line from La Fontaine’s Fables.

items.scope: The line people may be half-remembering
items.why: Machiavelli does have a famous sentence about deception, but it says the opposite thing — that deceivers never run short of victims: “he who seeks to deceive will always find someone who will allow himself to be deceived” (W. K. Marriott’s translation, Project Gutenberg ↗). That is about the gullible, not about the pleasure of turning the tables.
BrainyQuote ↗ and AZQuotes ↗ both serve the sentence under Machiavelli’s name without naming a work, a chapter or a translator.
The wording is established enough to head a 2023 British Journal of Social Psychology paper by Christian Blötner and Sebastian Bergold on Machiavellianism and bullshit production (PubMed record ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: It is La Fontaine’s, written in French and in verse: “Car c’est double plaisir de tromper le trompeur” — the last line of “Le Coq & le Renard,” Fables, Book II, fable 15 ↗.

context.heading: Why the line has an ending’s shape
lead: La Fontaine did not invent the story. A cock, a dog and a fox had been travelling together through Aesop, through the Buddhist Jataka tales, through the Thousand and One Nights, and into Renaissance Europe long before 1668. What he added was the exit line.

That is the trick of the Fables: the narrative is inherited, the epigram is his. Which is also why so many of his closing verses have escaped their fables and now circulate as free-floating aphorisms, ready to be pinned on whichever famous cynic the internet reaches for first.
detailsBody: Wikipedia’s article on the fable ↗ notes that the story appeared in Guillaume Gueroult’s first book of emblems (1550), prefaced with the summary “A trompeur, trompeur et demi” — to the trickster comes a trickster and a half. La Fontaine, it says, underlined his use of Gueroult by closing on a moral that echoed that source.

The fable’s comedy is in the cock’s deadpan. The fox announces universal peace; the cock replies that he is delighted, and mentions that two greyhounds are sprinting towards them, presumably with the same wonderful news. The fox remembers a pressing errand.
